en.title: Building: the whole course
en.short: What building covers, how building degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What building is
sections.text:
Building is the study and practice of constructing, maintaining and adapting the places where people live and work. It sits between architecture, which mainly designs the building, and civil engineering, which mainly designs the structure and the wider infrastructure. A building professional must understand materials, structures, services, cost, law and site safety, and must turn a drawing into a safe, usable building.

The subject matters because buildings are expensive, long-lasting and used by everyone. Mistakes can cost money, cause disputes or endanger people. These summaries teach principles. They do not replace a country’s building code, a contract or a qualified professional. Codes and regulations differ by country and change over time, so always check the current official source.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Programmes differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer a BSc in Building over about four years, while polytechnics usually offer an ND and then an HND, with industrial training between them. Nigerian courses typically include SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme, for this training. In the UK, building and construction management degrees are often three-year BSc courses, sometimes with a sandwich year in industry. Other countries have their own awards and lengths.

Professional registration differs. In Nigeria, engineering practice is regulated by COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria, and building has its own professional and registration arrangements. Do not assume one country’s rules apply in another. Check your department handbook for the exact award, length, industrial training requirements and the body that accredits your course.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics give you the tools. Mathematics for Building supports measurement and costing. Technical Drawing and Building Drawing teach you to read and produce plans, sections and details. Building Science explains heat, light, sound and moisture. Construction Materials covers the properties and uses of concrete, masonry, timber, steel and finishes. Statics explains forces, moments and equilibrium. Surveying covers levelling and setting out. Introduction to Building Construction shows how a building is put together. Communication and ICT, and Health and Safety on Site, are introduced early.

Core topics follow the building from the ground up. Substructure, Foundations and Groundworks come first. Building Structures introduces elements and simple design. Masonry and Concrete Superstructure, then Timber and Steel Framed Construction, follow. Roofs, floors, stairs and openings, finishes, joinery and partitions complete the fabric. Building Services covers water, drainage, electrical and fire services. Building Physics covers comfort, energy and environmental design. Construction Plant and Temporary Works, Measurement and Quantity Taking, Estimating and Cost Planning, Planning and Scheduling, Contracts and Procurement, Building Law and Regulation, and Professional Practice and Ethics support the work. The course ends with Research and the Final-Year Project.

At master’s level, advanced construction technology and digital construction, sustainable design, building performance simulation and research methods are common.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study with a pencil and a scale rule, not only a book. Redraw every drawing you are given, and add the dimensions and notes you would need on site. Keep a field notebook for site visits: record what you saw, how it was fixed and what you did not understand. Learn the units and typical values, such as the weight of concrete or the thickness of a wall, so that you notice when an answer is wrong.

Practise calculations by hand before using software. For measurement, take off a small building completely and check it against a known total. For planning, draw a simple bar chart and then a network. Read one current code or regulation for each topic, and note its country and date. Work in short, regular sessions; building is learned by repeated practice, not by last-minute reading.

keyPoints: Building is the study and practice of constructing and maintaining safe, usable buildings.
Degree lengths, awards and professional registration differ by country, so check your own handbook and current regulator.
Learn the building from the ground up: groundworks, structure, envelope, services and finishes.
Draw every detail, write units on every line, and check that answers are reasonable.
Understand the hand method and the current code before you trust software or an old note.
Measurement, cost, planning, law and ethics are part of building, not extras.

en.title: Mathematics for Building: Measurement and Checking
en.short: Arithmetic, algebra, geometry, trigonometry and mensuration for building measurement and checking.

sections.heading: Setting out calculations
sections.text: Write down what is known, what is asked and the unit of each quantity. Convert to one unit system first: 1 m = 1000 mm, 1 m² = 10,000 cm², 1 m³ = 1000 litres. Rearrange formulas with algebra before substituting numbers. For example, if V = l × w × d and V = 4.05 m³, l = 6.0 m, w = 4.5 m, then d = 4.05 ÷ (6.0 × 4.5) = 0.15 m. Check by multiplying back: 6.0 × 4.5 × 0.15 = 4.05 m³.

sections.heading: Areas and volumes
sections.text: Use consistent formulas. Rectangle area = length × breadth. Triangle area = ½ × base × height. Circle area = πr². Trapezium area = ½(a + b)h. Volume = area × depth for a prism. A 6.0 m × 4.5 m slab has area 27 m²; at 0.15 m thick its volume is 27 × 0.15 = 4.05 m³. Add wastage as a percentage: 5% of 4.05 = 0.2025, so order 4.2525 m³. For a cylinder, volume = πr²h.

sections.heading: Gradients and angles
sections.text: Gradient = rise ÷ run. A fall of 1.2 m over 15 m is 1.2 ÷ 15 = 0.08 = 8%, or 1 in 12.5. In trigonometry, label the right triangle: sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent. For a roof with 30° pitch and 4.0 m horizontal run, rise = 4.0 × tan 30° = 4.0 × 0.5774 = 2.31 m. Pythagoras gives rafter length = √(4.0² + 2.31²) = √(16 + 5.34) = 4.62 m.

sections.heading: Checking and statistics
sections.text: Check each answer by a second route: estimate, reverse the formula, or compare units. A mean is the sum of readings divided by their number. For five concrete cube strengths 24, 26, 25, 27, 28 N/mm², mean = 130 ÷ 5 = 26 N/mm². Percentage difference = difference ÷ original × 100. Keep significant figures sensible and state units. Codes and standards differ by country, so use the current local source for any permitted limit.

keyPoints: Convert all quantities to one unit system before calculating.
Area formulas: rectangle l × b, triangle ½ × base × height, circle πr²; volume of a prism = area × depth.
Gradient = rise ÷ run; percentage gradient = (rise ÷ run) × 100.
Trigonometry: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.
Mean = sum of readings ÷ number of readings; percentage = part ÷ whole × 100.
Check by reversing the formula, estimating and keeping units consistent.

en.title: Technical Drawing and Building Drawing
en.short: Orthographic views, plans, sections, elevations, scales, dimensioning, symbols, hand sketching and CAD basics.

sections.heading: Orthographic projection
sections.text: Orthographic projection shows a three-dimensional object by separate views projected at right angles onto planes. The front view, top view and side view are drawn in fixed positions. First-angle and third-angle projection place the views differently; the convention varies by country and office, so check the local standard before drawing. A drawing must be clear, consistent and to scale. Drawings for approval may need signatures from registered professionals; in Nigeria, for example, COREN regulates engineering registration.

sections.heading: Plans, sections, elevations
sections.text: A plan is a horizontal cut seen from above, usually taken about one metre above floor level. A section is a vertical cut that shows construction and heights. An elevation is an outside face seen straight on, without perspective. Cut lines, hatching and labels must match between views. These drawings let a builder set out walls, openings and levels.

sections.heading: Scale and dimensioning
sections.text: Scale is the ratio of drawing length to real length. At 1:50, a 40 mm line represents 40 × 50 = 2,000 mm, or 2 m. Dimensioning gives sizes with extension lines, dimension lines and arrowheads, in millimetres unless the standard says otherwise. Do not repeat a dimension in two views. Keep dimensions outside the drawing where possible, and give a title block with project, scale and date.

sections.heading: Symbols, sketching and CAD
sections.text: Symbols stand for doors, windows, materials and services; their meaning differs between countries, so use the local office or national standard. Hand sketching builds judgement of proportion: start with light construction lines, then firm outlines and thin dimension lines. Computer-aided drawing (CAD) uses layers, coordinates and model space to draw accurately. CAD does not replace standards; set line weights, text and symbols to the project standard.

keyPoints: Orthographic projection uses separate front, top and side views at right angles.
First-angle and third-angle projection differ; check the local drawing standard.
A plan is a horizontal cut, a section is a vertical cut, and an elevation is an outside face.
Scale = drawing length ÷ real length; at 1:50 a 40 mm line represents 2 m.
Dimension in millimetres unless the standard says otherwise, and do not duplicate dimensions.
Symbols and CAD settings must follow the local office or national standard.

en.title: Building Science: Heat, Light, Sound and Moisture
en.short: Thermal comfort, ventilation, daylight, acoustics and moisture movement, with simple calculations.

sections.heading: Heat and comfort
sections.text: Thermal comfort means feeling neither too warm nor too cool. It depends on air temperature, mean radiant temperature (average temperature of surrounding surfaces), air speed, relative humidity (vapour content compared with saturation at that temperature), clothing and activity. Heat flows from warm to cold. For steady state, Q = U A ΔT, where Q is heat flow in watts, U is thermal transmittance in W/(m²·K), A is area in m² and ΔT is temperature difference in kelvin. Comfort ranges vary.

sections.heading: Ventilation
sections.text: Ventilation replaces stale indoor air with outdoor air. It removes moisture, odours and pollutants. Volume flow rate is measured in m³/s. Air changes per hour (ACH) = flow rate × 3600 ÷ room volume. Example: a 60 m³ room with 0.03 m³/s has ACH = 0.03 × 3600 ÷ 60 = 1.8. Natural ventilation uses wind and temperature differences; mechanical ventilation uses fans. Required rates depend on room use and local regulations.

sections.heading: Daylight
sections.text: Daylight is natural light from the sky. Illuminance, in lux (lm/m²), is light falling on a surface. Daylight factor (DF) compares indoor and outdoor illuminance under a standard overcast sky: DF = indoor illuminance ÷ outdoor illuminance × 100%. Example: 300 lux indoors and 15,000 lux outdoors give DF = 300 ÷ 15,000 × 100 = 2%. Daylight depends on window size, position and room depth.

sections.heading: Sound and moisture
sections.text: Sound is a pressure wave. Sound pressure level is Lp = 20 log10(p ÷ p0), where p0 = 20 µPa. Example: p = 0.2 Pa gives Lp = 20 log10(0.2 ÷ 0.00002) = 80 dB. Reverberation time T = 0.161 V ÷ A, where V is volume in m³ and A is total absorption in m² sabins. Moisture moves as vapour from higher to lower vapour pressure. At the dew point air is saturated. Condensation occurs when a surface is below the dew point; ventilation and warming reduce it.

keyPoints: Thermal comfort depends on air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air speed, humidity, clothing and activity.
Heat flow: Q = U A ΔT, with Q in watts, U in W/(m²·K), A in m² and ΔT in kelvin.
Air changes per hour: ACH = flow rate × 3600 ÷ room volume, with flow in m³/s and volume in m³.
Daylight factor: DF = indoor illuminance ÷ outdoor illuminance × 100%.
Sound pressure level is Lp = 20 log10(p ÷ p0) with p0 = 20 µPa; reverberation time is T = 0.161 V ÷ A.
Condensation occurs when a surface temperature is below the dew point of the air.

en.title: Construction Materials: Properties, Selection and Testing
en.short: Properties, selection and basic tests of concrete, masonry, timber, steel, glass, plastics and bitumen.

sections.heading: Properties and selection
sections.text: Every material is chosen for strength, stiffness, durability, fire behaviour, maintenance and cost. Strength resists load; stiffness resists deformation. Durability is how well a material keeps its properties under weather, moisture, chemicals and use. Fire behaviour covers combustibility, smoke and loss of strength when hot. Cost includes purchase, fixing, maintenance and expected life, not only price per unit. Codes and standards differ by country, so check the project specification and local building code before selection.

sections.heading: Concrete and masonry
sections.text: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel bars carry tension in reinforced concrete. Its properties depend on cement, aggregates, water and curing. Too much water lowers strength and raises shrinkage. Masonry units, bricks and blocks, are strong in compression and weak in tension; mortar joins them and affects weather tightness. Fired clay bricks resist fire and moisture well, while concrete blocks are often cheaper. Both need sound units and mortar.

sections.heading: Timber, steel and glass
sections.text: Timber is light, strong along the grain and renewable, but it burns, decays when wet and changes size with moisture. Its moisture content and grade must suit the use. Steel is strong in tension and compression, but it corrodes unless protected and loses strength in fire. Glass is brittle and transparent; ordinary glass breaks into sharp pieces, so safety glass is used where people may hit it. It is a poor insulator and cracks under thermal shock.

sections.heading: Plastics, bitumen and testing
sections.text: Plastics are light and resist corrosion, but many soften when hot, burn with smoke and expand more than metals. Bitumen is waterproof and used in damp-proofing, roofing and roads; it softens when hot and becomes brittle when cold. Basic tests include slump and cube crushing for concrete, water absorption for masonry, moisture content for timber, tensile tests for steel, impact for glass, flammability for plastics, and penetration or softening point for bitumen. Example: a 150 mm cube fails at 450 kN. Area = 150 × 150 = 22,500 mm². Stress = 450,000 ÷ 22,500 = 20 N/mm².

keyPoints: Select materials by strength, stiffness, durability, fire behaviour, maintenance and whole-life cost, not price alone.
Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, so steel bars carry tension in reinforced concrete.
Masonry is strong in compression and weak in tension; sound units and mortar improve durability.
Timber burns and decays, steel corrodes and loses strength in fire, and ordinary glass is brittle.
Plastics are light and corrosion resistant but may soften, burn and expand when hot; bitumen is waterproof but softens when hot.
Cube compressive stress = failure load ÷ cube area, and basic tests include slump, water absorption, moisture content, tensile, impact, flammability and bitumen tests.

en.title: Statics: Forces, Moments and Equilibrium
en.short: Forces, moments, reactions, free-body diagrams and simple beam and frame equilibrium.

sections.heading: Forces and diagrams
sections.text: A force is a push or pull with magnitude, direction and point of application, measured in newtons (N) or kilonewtons (kN). A free-body diagram (FBD) isolates one body and shows every external force on it, including support reactions. Supports are replaced by the forces they provide: a roller gives one reaction perpendicular to its surface, a pin gives two components, and a fixed support gives two components plus a moment.

sections.heading: Moments and reactions
sections.text:
A moment is the turning effect of a force: M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot, in N·m. For equilibrium, ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0. These equations find reactions.

Example: a simply supported beam spans 6 m. A 12 kN load acts 2 m from left support A. Taking moments about A: RB × 6 = 12 × 2, so RB = 4 kN. ΣFy gives RA = 12 − 4 = 8 kN. Check about B: 8 × 6 = 12 × 4 = 48 kN·m.

sections.heading: Frames and load paths
sections.text: In a simple pin-jointed frame or truss, loads at joints make members carry axial tension or compression. Each joint must satisfy equilibrium. In buildings, loads follow a path: roof or floor to beams, beams to columns or walls, then to foundations and ground. A floor area 4 m × 3 m carrying 5 kN/m² has total load 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 kN. If two beams share it equally, each carries 30 kN; real sharing varies.

sections.heading: Towards design
sections.text: Statics gives the demands on a structure: reactions, bending moments, shear and axial forces. Later design compares these demands with the resistance of chosen materials and sections, using safety factors. Codes and safety factors differ between countries, so check the local code. Clear FBDs and load paths make later checks easier and reduce missed loads.

keyPoints: A force has magnitude, direction and point of application; a free-body diagram shows all external forces and reactions on one body.
Moment M = F × d, with d measured perpendicular to the force.
For equilibrium: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0.
A roller gives one reaction, a pin two components, and a fixed support two components plus a moment.
For a simply supported beam, take moments about one support to find the other reaction, then use ΣFy = 0.
Loads travel from slabs or roofs to beams, then columns or walls, then foundations; statics gives demands for later design.

en.title: Surveying: Levelling and Setting Out
en.short: Levelling, distance and angle measurement, coordinates, and setting out buildings on site.

sections.heading: Levelling
sections.text:
Levelling finds height differences. A datum is a fixed reference height; reduced level (RL) is a height measured from it. In the height of instrument method, a backsight is a staff reading on a point of known RL, and a foresight is a reading on the point whose RL you want. Instrument height = RL + backsight, and a new RL = instrument height − foresight.

Example: RL of A = 100.000 m, backsight 1.250 m, foresight 1.800 m.
Instrument height = 100.000 + 1.250 = 101.250 m
RL of B = 101.250 − 1.800 = 99.450 m

Close a levelling run back onto a known point. The closing error is the difference between the final and known RL, and it must be within the limit set for the job.

sections.heading: Distance and angles
sections.text:
A tape is simple but needs tension and level ground; electronic distance measurement (EDM) in a total station is faster. Slope distance must be reduced to horizontal distance: horizontal = √(slope² − height difference²).

Example: slope 25.000 m, height difference 1.500 m.
Horizontal = √(25.000² − 1.500²) = √(625.000 − 2.250) = √622.750 = 24.955 m

Angles are measured with a theodolite or total station. A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north. The 3-4-5 rule checks a right angle: a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 units has a right angle between the 3 and 4 sides.

sections.heading: Coordinates and setting out
sections.text:
Coordinates locate points by easting and northing on a chosen grid. Grids differ between countries and projects, so state the system and datum used. From coordinates you can calculate bearing and distance.

Example: from (E 1000.000, N 2000.000) to (E 1030.000, N 2040.000).
ΔE = 30.000 m, ΔN = 40.000 m
Distance = √(30² + 40²) = 50.000 m
Bearing = arctan(30 ÷ 40) = 36.87° from north

Setting out transfers the drawing to the ground. Establish a baseline, then set corners by distance and angle or by coordinates. Check each rectangle by its diagonals, which must be equal.

sections.heading: Checks and rules
sections.text: Practical checks: close every levelling run, repeat measurements, check the instrument, and compare set-out dimensions with the drawing before work starts. Instruments, coordinate systems and regulations vary by country. In Nigeria, COREN registers engineers, and surveying is a separately regulated profession; check the current local rules.

keyPoints: Height of instrument = RL + backsight; new RL = height of instrument − foresight.
Closing error = measured final RL − known RL, and must be within the job limit.
Horizontal distance = √(slope² − height difference²).
Distance = √(ΔE² + ΔN²); bearing = arctan(ΔE ÷ ΔN), adjusted for the quadrant.
Check set-out by equal diagonals and by closing measurements.
Instruments, coordinate systems and professional registration vary by country.

en.title: Introduction to Building Construction
en.short: The sequence of building work, main trades, site roles and why codes and registration vary by country.

sections.heading: Sequence of work
sections.text: Building work usually follows a sequence, though some tasks overlap. Site preparation clears the plot, sets levels and provides access, storage and temporary services. Substructure is the part below ground, including foundations and ground floors. Superstructure is the part above ground: columns, walls, beams and floors. Enclosure makes the building weathertight through roof, external walls, windows and doors. Finishes are the final surfaces and fittings: plaster, paint, tiles and joinery. Services are connected as the work proceeds. Each stage should be checked before the next covers it.

sections.heading: Trades and roles
sections.text: Main trades include bricklayers, carpenters, concrete workers, steel fixers, plumbers, electricians, plasterers, tilers and painters. Site roles differ by contract. The client pays for the work. The architect designs and administers the contract. The engineer designs and checks the structure and services. The quantity surveyor measures and controls cost. The contractor builds, with a site manager, foremen and a safety officer. Labourers support the trades.

sections.heading: Codes and registration
sections.text: Design codes, standards and professional registration differ between countries. In Nigeria, for example, COREN registers engineers, while architects and builders have their own registration bodies. Always check the current national code and the local approving authority. Do not assume one country’s rules apply elsewhere.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Consider a made-up two-room clinic in Ibadan. The client appoints an architect and a quantity surveyor. Site preparation clears the plot. The substructure uses strip foundations. The superstructure is sandcrete (sand and cement) block walls with a timber roof. Enclosure adds windows and doors. Finishes include plaster, paint and floor tiles. Plumbers and electricians connect water and power. The site manager checks each stage against the drawings and the national code. This order is typical, not fixed.

keyPoints: Building work usually moves from site preparation to substructure, superstructure, enclosure and finishes.
Substructure is below ground; superstructure is above ground.
Main trades include bricklayers, carpenters, concrete workers, steel fixers, plumbers, electricians, plasterers, tilers and painters.
Site roles include client, architect, engineer, quantity surveyor, contractor, site manager and safety officer.
Design codes, standards and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria COREN regulates engineering.
Always check the current national code and local approving authority before relying on a rule.

en.title: Communication and ICT for Building
en.short: Reports, letters, drawings, spreadsheets, databases, presentations and shared digital building models.

sections.heading: Reports and letters
sections.text: ICT means information and communication technology: the tools used to create, store and send information. A technical report records work in a clear order, usually title, summary, introduction, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references. It should be accurate and easy to check. A formal letter has a date, reference, recipient, subject and a clear request. Keep sentences short and attach only what the reader needs.

sections.heading: Drawings and presentations
sections.text: Drawings communicate shape, size and location. A drawing for communication needs a title block, scale, north point, dimensions and revision number. It is not a substitute for the technical drawing rules you learn elsewhere. A presentation should make one main point per slide, use large readable text and simple images, and end with a clear decision or next step. A short case: a site team receives a revised drawing. The revision number and date tell them which sheet is current, so they do not build from an old copy.

sections.heading: Spreadsheets and databases
sections.text: A spreadsheet stores numbers in rows and columns and calculates with formulas. Use it for schedules, quantities and simple cost checks. Always label units and check formulas. A database stores related records in tables and answers queries, such as a list of doors by floor. Example: 12 doors at ₦85,000 each. The formula =12*85000 gives ₦1,020,000. If one door is added, change the count to 13; the total becomes ₦1,105,000. Check: 13 × 85,000 = 1,105,000.

sections.heading: Digital models and sharing
sections.text: A digital model is a computer representation of a building. Building Information Modelling (BIM) is a way of working in which shared models carry geometry and information, such as room names and material data. Information sharing needs agreed file names, versions, permissions and backups. Software and data standards vary by country and organisation, so agree them at the start. Professional registration, such as COREN in Nigeria, and design codes also differ by country. A common data environment is a controlled store for project information; check the project’s rules before uploading.

keyPoints: A technical report presents work in a clear, checkable order.
Formal letters need a date, reference, subject and a clear request.
Drawings communicate through title blocks, scales, dimensions and revision numbers.
Spreadsheets calculate with formulas; label units and check every formula.
Databases store related records and answer queries.
Digital models and BIM share building information; agree file names, versions and standards because software and data standards vary.

en.title: Health, Safety and the Construction Site
en.short: This summary covers hazards, risk assessment, PPE, safe access, scaffolding, first aid and site induction.

sections.heading: Hazards and risk
sections.text:
A hazard is anything that can cause harm. A risk is the chance of harm and how serious it could be. Common hazards include falls from height, slips and trips, falling objects, manual handling, noise, dust, electricity, moving plant, excavation collapse and harmful substances.

Risk assessment means identifying hazards, deciding who may be harmed, and choosing controls. Many organisations rate risk as likelihood × severity; if both are scored 1 to 5, a fall scored 4 × 5 = 20 is high. Check local law.

sections.heading: Controls and PPE
sections.text:
Controls follow a hierarchy: remove the hazard, substitute a safer method, use engineering controls such as guardrails, organise work safely, then use personal protective equipment (PPE). PPE is the last line of defence. It includes a hard hat, safety boots, high-visibility clothing, gloves, eye protection, hearing protection and respiratory protection. PPE must fit, suit the task and be checked. It does not remove the hazard.

In Nigeria, the Factories Act and the Employees’ Compensation Act are examples; other countries have their own laws. Check current local regulations.

sections.heading: Access and scaffolds
sections.text:
Safe access means a clear, firm and lit route to every workplace. Open edges and openings need guards. Ladders are for short work, must be secured and are not a long-term work platform.

Scaffolding awareness means knowing the basics, not designing scaffolds. A scaffold needs a stable base, standards, ledgers, guardrails, toe boards and safe access. Competent people erect, alter and inspect it. Never climb the frame or remove a guardrail. Report missing parts.

sections.heading: Induction and first aid
sections.text:
Site induction introduces a new worker to the layout, hazards, traffic routes, PPE rules, emergency alarms, assembly points and reporting. It should be recorded, and no worker should start without it.

First aid needs a trained first aider, a stocked kit, emergency numbers and a procedure for calling an ambulance. Workers should know where the kit is and how to report injuries and near misses, because near misses warn of danger before someone is hurt.

keyPoints: A hazard is a source of harm; risk is the chance and seriousness of harm.
Risk assessment identifies hazards, who may be harmed and the controls needed.
Controls follow a hierarchy, and PPE is the last line of defence.
Safe access and correctly erected, inspected scaffolds help prevent falls.
Site induction and first-aid arrangements must be in place before work starts.
Safety law differs by country; in Nigeria the Factories Act and Employees’ Compensation Act are examples, so check current local regulations.

en.title: Substructure, Foundations and Groundworks
en.short: Site clearance, excavation and support, foundation types, damp-proofing, hardcore and ground drainage.

sections.heading: Site clearance and excavation
sections.text:
Substructure is the part of a building below ground level. Groundworks prepare for it. Site clearance removes vegetation, topsoil, rubbish and old structures. Topsoil is weak and compressible, so it is stripped and often kept for landscaping. Setting out fixes lines and levels before excavation.

Excavation removes soil to reach a bearing stratum or formation level. Trenches are narrow excavations for strip foundations or services. In loose or wet ground they can collapse, so trench support such as timbering, sheeting or proprietary boxes is used. Keep edges clear, provide safe access and check for buried services.

sections.heading: Foundation types
sections.text:
A foundation transfers load from the building to the ground without excessive settlement. A strip foundation is a continuous concrete strip under a wall or row of columns. A pad foundation is an isolated block under a single column. A raft is a slab covering the footprint, useful where soil is weak or loads are uneven. A pile is a deep member that carries load to stronger soil or rock, or gains friction along its shaft.

Selection depends on load and ground. Firm ground at shallow depth suits strips and pads. Weak or variable ground may need a raft or piles. Piles are also used where shallow foundations would be uneconomic or settlement must be limited. Foundation design codes differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN registers engineers, so check the national code and local rules.

sections.heading: Damp-proofing and drainage
sections.text:
Damp-proofing stops moisture rising into the building. A damp-proof course (DPC) is a barrier in walls near floor level. A damp-proof membrane (DPM) is a sheet under a ground floor slab. Hardcore is compacted broken stone below the slab; it gives a stable base and must be well graded and compacted.

Ground drainage removes water. Surface water drains take rainwater away; land drains lower the water table near foundations. A clinic on firm sandy soil might use strip foundations, a DPC, a DPM over hardcore and a perimeter drain.

keyPoints: Substructure is the part below ground level, and groundworks prepare the site for it.
Site clearance removes weak topsoil, and setting out fixes lines and levels before excavation.
Trench support prevents collapse in loose or wet ground, and excavations need safe access and checks for buried services.
Strip and pad foundations suit firm shallow ground, while rafts and piles suit weak or variable ground or heavy loads.
A DPC and DPM stop rising damp, hardcore gives a compacted base, and ground drainage removes water.
Foundation design codes and professional registration rules differ by country, so check the national code and local requirements.

en.title: Building Structures: Elements and Simple Design
en.short: Loads, load paths and simple sizing checks for beams, columns, slabs, walls and foundations.

sections.heading: Loads and paths
sections.text: Buildings carry dead load (self-weight of structure and finishes), live load (people, furniture, stored goods), and environmental loads such as wind or snow. Loads travel along a load path: floor slab to beams, beams to columns or walls, then to foundations and the ground. A continuous path and clear transfer at each junction are essential. Design codes and permitted limits vary by country, so check the national code and local registration, for example COREN in Nigeria.

sections.heading: Elements and checks
sections.text: Beams resist bending and shear. For a simply supported beam, maximum bending moment under uniform load w over span L is M = wL² ÷ 8. Elastic bending stress is σ = M ÷ Z, where Z is the section modulus, a property of the cross-section. Deflection is checked because a beam can be strong but too flexible. Columns carry axial compression; stress is P ÷ A, and slender columns must be checked for buckling. Slabs span one way or two ways and transfer load to supports. Loadbearing walls carry compression and need adequate thickness and restraint. Foundations spread load so bearing pressure q = P ÷ A does not exceed the safe bearing capacity of the soil; settlement also matters.

sections.heading: Worked check
sections.text: Example: a simply supported floor beam spans L = 4.0 m and carries w = 12 kN/m. M = 12 × 4² ÷ 8 = 24 kN·m. Choose a timber section with Z = 800,000 mm³. Convert: M = 24 × 10⁶ N·mm. σ = 24,000,000 ÷ 800,000 = 30 N/mm². If the permitted bending stress is 12 N/mm², the section is too small; a larger Z is needed. Check shear and deflection separately. Preliminary sizing rules, such as span-to-depth ratios, are guides only and vary with material, support and code.

keyPoints: The load path runs from slab to beam to column or wall to foundation to ground.
For a simply supported beam under uniform load, M = wL² ÷ 8 and bending stress is σ = M ÷ Z.
Column axial stress is P ÷ A, and slender columns must also be checked for buckling.
Foundation bearing pressure is q = P ÷ A and must not exceed the safe bearing capacity of the soil.
Deflection, shear and settlement can control a design even when bending stress is acceptable.
Design codes, permitted limits and professional registration vary by country; check the national code and local body such as COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Masonry and Concrete Superstructure
en.short: Brickwork, blockwork, mortar, bonding, formwork, reinforcement, concrete placing, curing and defects.

sections.heading: Masonry and mortar
sections.text: Brickwork uses burnt clay or calcium silicate bricks; blockwork uses concrete, sandcrete or stabilised earth blocks. Units and mortar must suit the local climate and be checked against the national code. Mortar is a mix of cement, sand, lime and water. It binds units, fills joints and allows movement. It should not be stronger than the units. Bonding means overlapping units so vertical joints do not line up; stretcher and English bonds are common. Movement joints are vertical gaps with compressible filler and sealant. They absorb thermal and moisture movement. Spacing depends on material and code.

sections.heading: Formwork and reinforcement
sections.text: Formwork is the temporary mould for wet concrete. It must be strong, rigid and tight, with release agent, and be struck only when the concrete can carry loads. Reinforcement is steel bar or mesh placed as drawings show. Cover is the concrete between bar and surface; it protects steel from corrosion and fire. Laps, spacers and tying keep bars in place. Check bar size, position and cover before pouring.

sections.heading: Placing and curing
sections.text: Place concrete near its final position and avoid dropping it far, which causes segregation. Compact with a vibrator or rod to remove air voids. Curing keeps moisture and a suitable temperature so cement hydrates and gains strength. Methods include water, wet covers and curing compounds; hot, dry or windy weather needs extra care. Example: a slab 4.0 m × 3.0 m × 0.15 m needs 4.0 × 3.0 × 0.15 = 1.8 m³. A 5% waste allowance gives 1.8 × 1.05 = 1.89 m³.

sections.heading: Quality and defects
sections.text: Quality control checks units, mortar, dimensions, plumb, level, formwork, bar cover and curing. Common defects include honeycombing from poor compaction, cold joints from delayed pours, cracks from movement or shrinkage, efflorescence (white salt deposits) from soluble salts, and damp penetration. In hot climates, shade materials and cure early; in wet climates, protect fresh work. Codes, standards and registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration. Check the national code and specification.

keyPoints: Mortar binds masonry units and should not be stronger than them.
Bonding overlaps units to avoid continuous vertical joints; movement joints absorb thermal and moisture movement.
Formwork must be strong, rigid and tight; reinforcement needs correct size, position and cover.
Concrete must be placed without segregation, compacted to remove air, and cured to gain strength.
Concrete volume = length × width × thickness; add a waste allowance. Example: 4.0 × 3.0 × 0.15 = 1.8 m³.
Quality control and national codes vary by country; check the specification and local registration rules.

en.title: Timber and Steel Framed Construction
en.short: Timber and steel frames, roof structures, connections, bracing, fire and corrosion protection.

sections.heading: Timber frames
sections.text: Timber frames use sawn or engineered timber members. Platform framing builds one storey at a time; balloon framing runs studs through two storeys. Studs are vertical members, and sheathing or diagonal bracing gives lateral stability. Glued laminated timber (glulam) and cross-laminated timber (CLT) are engineered products that allow longer spans. Timber is light, renewable and easy to work, but it must be kept dry and protected from decay and insects. Permitted heights and design rules differ by country.

sections.heading: Steel frames
sections.text: Steel frames use hot-rolled beams and columns, often with concrete floors acting compositely. Steel is strong, precise and fast to erect, and it spans far. It is dense, conducts heat and loses strength in fire, so it needs fire protection. It also corrodes if unprotected. Stability comes from bracing or rigid joints.

sections.heading: Roofs, connections, bracing
sections.text: Roof structures may be timber trussed rafters or steel trusses with purlins. Purlins are horizontal members that support rafters or roof covering. Bracing resists wind and prevents racking, the sideways distortion of a frame. Connections transfer forces: nails, screws, bolts and nail plates in timber; bolts, welds and plates in steel. Connections often govern design. In a made-up case, a two-storey clinic in Kumasi, Ghana, uses a steel frame with timber roof trusses; bolted bases and diagonal roof bracing carry wind, and treated timber is kept clear of wet areas.

sections.heading: Fire, corrosion and codes
sections.text: Fire: timber chars, and the char layer slows burning; large sections can keep strength for a useful time. Steel softens quickly when hot. Steel is protected by boards, sprays or intumescent coatings; timber by adequate section size, encapsulation or sprinklers. Corrosion: steel is galvanised or painted; timber is treated with preservative and detailed to shed water. Structural design and fire rules are country-specific. Europe uses Eurocodes 3 and 5 for steel and timber; the United States uses the AISC steel specification and NDS for wood; Nigeria’s Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN) registers engineers. Check the local code.

keyPoints: Timber is light, renewable and workable but needs protection from moisture, decay and insects.
Steel is strong, precise and fast to erect but needs fire and corrosion protection.
Roof trusses and purlins carry roof loads, while bracing resists wind and racking.
Connections such as nails, screws, bolts, welds and plates often govern frame design.
Timber chars in fire; steel loses strength when hot, so both need fire protection.
Structural design codes and fire regulations differ by country, so check the local code and use a registered engineer.

en.title: Roofs and Roof Coverings
en.short: Pitched and flat roofs, trusses, purlins, coverings, insulation, ventilation, waterproofing and rainwater disposal.

sections.heading: Roof form and slope
sections.text:
A pitched roof has sloping surfaces that shed water. A flat roof is nominally level but has a slight fall, often 1:40 to 1:80, to drains. Slope is written as a ratio of rise to run or as an angle. Minimum slope depends on the covering and climate. Codes differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering practice, and designers check the National Building Code. Always check the current local code.

Example: a roof rises 1.5 m over a run of 6 m.
Pitch ratio = 1.5:6 = 1:4.
Angle = arctan(1.5 ÷ 6) = arctan(0.25) = 14.0°.

sections.heading: Trusses and purlins
sections.text:
A roof truss is a triangulated frame, usually timber or steel, that carries roof loads to the walls. Purlins are horizontal members fixed across trusses to support the covering or sheeting.

Purlins span between trusses. Their spacing depends on the covering, load and code; follow the manufacturer and local rules. Bracing keeps the roof stable against wind.

sections.heading: Coverings and insulation
sections.text:
Common coverings include clay or concrete tiles, slate, metal sheets and membranes. Choice depends on slope, climate, weight, cost and fire performance.

Insulation slows heat flow; it may sit on the ceiling or above the roof deck. Ventilation removes moisture. Cold roofs need ventilation to prevent condensation; warm roofs place insulation above the deck. In hot climates, reflective surfaces and ventilation reduce heat gain.

sections.heading: Waterproofing and drainage
sections.text:
Waterproofing uses membranes, flashing and sealed joints. Rainwater is collected in gutters and taken by downpipes to drains. Size them from roof area and local rainfall intensity.

Example: a roof plan area of 100 m² receives rain at 150 mm/h.
Flow = 100 × 0.15 = 15 m³/h.
In litres per second: 15 × 1000 ÷ 3600 = 4.17 L/s.
Rainfall intensity varies by place and return period, so use local data.

keyPoints: Pitched roofs shed water by slope; flat roofs need a fall to drains.
A roof truss is a triangulated frame; purlins span between trusses to support the covering.
Covering choice depends on slope, climate, weight and cost; follow the manufacturer and local code.
Insulation and ventilation together control heat and condensation; cold and warm roof details differ.
Rainwater flow = roof plan area × rainfall intensity; convert units carefully.
Minimum slopes, thermal limits and rainfall data vary by country and year; check current official sources.

en.title: Floors, Stairs and Openings
en.short: Ground and suspended floors, stair geometry with a worked example, ramps, lintels, openings and edge protection.

sections.heading: Floors
sections.text: A ground floor is supported directly by the ground, usually a concrete slab on hardcore with a damp-proof membrane. A suspended floor is carried by walls or beams, leaving a void below; it may be timber joists or concrete, and a timber floor’s void needs ventilation to prevent rot. Floors carry dead load, the weight of the floor itself and anything fixed to it, and imposed load, people and furniture, safely and without excessive deflection. Openings in floors need trimming and support.

sections.heading: Stair geometry
sections.text:
Stairs link levels by steps. The riser is the vertical rise of one step, the going is the horizontal tread depth, and the pitch is the angle of the flight. A flight runs between landings. Total rise = number of risers × riser height. The number of goings is one fewer than the number of risers when the top step reaches a floor level. A common comfort guide is 2R + G between about 550 and 700 mm, but legal limits differ by country.

Example: total rise 2700 mm. Use riser R = 180 mm. Risers = 2700 ÷ 180 = 15. Goings = 14. With going G = 280 mm, total going = 14 × 280 = 3920 mm. Pitch = arctan(180 ÷ 280) = 32.7°. Check: 2R + G = 2 × 180 + 280 = 640 mm.

sections.heading: Ramps and openings
sections.text: A ramp is an inclined surface for wheelchairs, trolleys or level changes. Its slope is stated as a ratio such as 1:12 or a percentage; accessible gradients, landings and handrails are set by national rules. A lintel is a beam over an opening that carries the wall or floor above. Openings for doors, windows, stairs and services interrupt continuity, so they need lintels, trimming joists or framing. Headroom and opening sizes also vary by country.

sections.heading: Edge protection
sections.text: Edge protection guards people and objects at floor edges, stair openings, shafts and ramps. In completed buildings it includes guardrails, balustrades and handrails; during construction it includes temporary barriers, toe boards and fixed covers over openings. Guard heights, gap sizes and loadings differ by country, so check the current national building code and site safety rules. A cover should be fixed and marked, not merely laid over the hole.

keyPoints: A ground floor bears on the ground; a suspended floor is carried by walls or beams with a void below, ventilated when the floor is timber.
For simple stairs, total rise = number of risers × riser height, and goings = risers − 1 when the top step meets a floor.
A common comfort guide is 2R + G between about 550 and 700 mm, but legal stair limits differ by country.
Pitch = arctan(riser ÷ going); for R = 180 mm and G = 280 mm the pitch is 32.7°.
Lintels and trimming carry loads around openings in walls and floors.
Guardrails, balustrades and temporary edge protection must follow the current national code; heights and gaps vary by country.

en.title: Finishes, Joinery and Partitions
en.short: Plaster, screed, tiling, painting, ceilings, partitions, doors, windows and basic joinery.

sections.heading: Substrate and moisture
sections.text:
A finish is only as good as what it sits on. The substrate is the surface receiving the finish: masonry, concrete, timber or a board. It must be clean, sound and dry enough for the product. Moisture is the main enemy. Water trapped under a screed, tile bed or paint film causes blistering, mould, salt staining and loss of adhesion. Damp-proof courses and ventilation help, but the finish must also be able to dry. Movement joints absorb thermal and moisture movement so finishes do not crack.

Maintenance starts at design: choose a finish that suits the exposure, and leave a way to inspect and repair it.

sections.heading: Wet and applied finishes
sections.text:
Plaster is a wet mix of gypsum, lime or cement with sand, spread on walls and ceilings to give a level, paintable surface. Gypsum plaster suits dry internal walls; cement-based render suits external work. Screed is a levelling layer of cement and sand over a concrete floor. It must cure and dry before tiling. Tiles are fixed with adhesive or mortar, with grout and movement gaps. Painting needs a dry, primed surface, and the paint type and number of coats depend on the exposure.

Example: a 20 mm screed over 30 m² needs 30 × 0.020 = 0.6 m³ of wet mix, before allowing for wastage.

sections.heading: Ceilings, partitions and joinery
sections.text: Ceilings hide services and improve acoustics and fire resistance. Common types are plasterboard on a metal grid and timber boards. Partitions divide space without carrying the main structure: stud partitions of timber or steel with board facing, or lightweight blockwork. Joinery is the craft of making and fitting timber parts such as doors, windows, frames and stairs. Doors and windows must be correctly sized, hung, sealed and drained. Durability and maintenance depend on matching the finish to the exposure and checking seals and coatings.

keyPoints: A finish depends on a clean, sound, suitably dry substrate.
Trapped moisture causes blistering, mould and loss of adhesion.
Screed must cure and dry before tiling.
Partitions divide space but do not carry the main structure.
Joinery covers the making and fitting of timber doors, windows and frames.
Durability depends on matching the finish to exposure and maintaining seals.

en.title: Building Services: Water, Drainage, Electrical and Fire
en.short: Water supply, drainage, plumbing, electrical distribution, lighting, ventilation, air conditioning and fire safety.

sections.heading: Water and plumbing
sections.text: Building services are the systems that make a building usable. Potable water is fit to drink. A water supply brings it from the main or a storage tank to taps through pipes, valves and pumps. Plumbing covers this pipework, fittings and traps. Hot and cold supplies need pressure and insulation. Services must be coordinated with structure and finishes: pipes pass through sleeves in walls and slabs, and risers need space. Water quality and plumbing rules vary by country.

sections.heading: Sanitary drainage
sections.text: Sanitary drainage carries sewage and waste water away. A trap holds a water seal that stops sewer gas entering. Drain pipes fall at a gradient, and vents protect the seal. Inspection chambers give access for clearing blockages. Drainage needs space below floors, so it must be planned with foundations and structure. Pipe sizes, gradients and materials are set by national regulations, which vary.

sections.heading: Electrical and lighting
sections.text: Electrical distribution takes power from the supply point to a distribution board, then through circuits to outlets. Earthing and protective devices reduce shock and fire risk. A demand factor allows for loads that do not all run at once. Example: a connected load of 12 kW with a demand factor of 0.6 gives a maximum demand of 12 × 0.6 = 7.2 kW. Lighting uses lumens for light output and lux for light on a surface. Cables must be sized for current and voltage drop.

sections.heading: Air and fire
sections.text: Ventilation supplies fresh air and removes pollutants, by natural openings or fans. Air conditioning controls temperature, humidity and cleanliness. Fire detection uses smoke or heat detectors linked to an alarm. Fire protection includes passive measures, such as compartmentation (dividing the building into fire-resistant sections) and protected escape routes, and active measures, such as sprinklers and extinguishers. Ducts and cables need ceiling and floor voids. Fire-stopping seals openings where services pass through fire-resistant walls and floors. Standards vary by country; for example, COREN regulates engineering registration in Nigeria.

keyPoints: Building services must be coordinated with structure and finishes from the start.
Potable water is fit to drink; plumbing carries it through pipes, valves and traps.
A trap water seal stops sewer gas entering sanitary drainage; vents protect the seal.
Maximum demand = connected load × demand factor.
Lighting design uses lumens and lux, and cables must be sized for current and voltage drop.
Fire protection combines detection, passive compartmentation and active systems such as sprinklers, and service standards vary by country.

en.title: Building Physics: Comfort, Energy and Environmental Design
en.short: Applied thermal, ventilation, daylight, acoustic and moisture design for comfort and low energy use.

sections.heading: Thermal comfort and passive design
sections.text:
Comfort depends on air temperature, mean radiant temperature, humidity, air speed and clothing/activity. Operative temperature combines air and radiant temperature. Passive design first reduces demand: orientation, shading, insulation, thermal mass and controlled openings. In hot climates, shade and cross-ventilation matter; in cool climates, insulation and airtightness matter. Check local code and climate data.

Fabric heat loss is Q = U A ΔT, where U is thermal transmittance (W/m²K), A area and ΔT temperature difference. Example: a 20 m² wall with U = 0.30 W/m²K and ΔT = 10 K loses Q = 0.30 × 20 × 10 = 60 W. Halving U to 0.15 saves 30 W.

sections.heading: Ventilation and moisture
sections.text: Ventilation removes pollutants and moisture and supplies fresh air. Air change rate n = Q ÷ V, where Q is airflow (m³/h) and V room volume (m³). A 60 m³ room with 30 m³/h has n = 0.5 air changes per hour. Moisture control avoids condensation: warm moist air must not meet cold surfaces. Use vapour control layers, drainage, dry construction and adequate ventilation. Psychrometric charts link temperature, humidity and dew point; check local standards for required rates.

sections.heading: Daylight and acoustics
sections.text: Daylight factor DF = indoor illuminance ÷ outdoor horizontal illuminance × 100%. It varies with sky, window size, glazing and room depth. Use daylight from two sides where possible, light shelves and shading against glare and heat. Reverberation time is T = 0.161 V ÷ A, where V is room volume (m³) and A total absorption (m² sabins). Example: V = 120 m³, A = 20 m² gives T = 0.161 × 120 ÷ 20 = 0.966 s, about 0.97 s. Add absorbent surfaces to reduce noise.

sections.heading: Checking design
sections.text: Combine checks early. A room may meet daylight but overheat; ventilation may control moisture but waste energy. Use simple calculations, then confirm with local regulations and, for larger projects, simulation. Standards and professional registration differ by country, for example COREN in Nigeria; check the current national code.

keyPoints: Fabric heat loss is Q = U A ΔT; reducing U or ΔT lowers energy use.
Air change rate is n = Q ÷ V, and ventilation controls moisture and pollutants.
Daylight factor is DF = indoor illuminance ÷ outdoor horizontal illuminance × 100%.
Reverberation time is T = 0.161 V ÷ A in metric units.
Passive design uses orientation, shading, insulation, thermal mass and controlled openings before mechanical systems.
Codes, comfort standards and registration differ by country; check the current national source.

en.title: Construction Plant, Temporary Works and Site Safety
en.short: Plant selection, earthmoving, lifting, concrete, formwork, scaffolding and site safety.

sections.heading: Choosing plant
sections.text: Construction plant means the machines used on site, as distinct from permanent materials. Selection depends on task, ground, access, output and cost. Hiring suits short or varied work; owning suits steady demand. Output depends on cycle time: output = load volume × cycles per hour × efficiency. Operators must be trained and competent, and the area kept clear.

sections.heading: Earthmoving and compaction
sections.text:
Excavators dig and load; loaders scoop and carry; bulldozers push; dumpers haul. Match machine to haul distance and material. Compaction removes air voids, raising density and reducing settlement. Rollers, vibratory plates and rammers are chosen by soil and space.

Example: a 1.0 m³ bucket, 30 s cycle, fill factor 0.9 (how full the bucket is) and 50 productive minutes per hour gives 1.0 × 0.9 × (3600 ÷ 30) × (50 ÷ 60) = 90 m³ per hour loose. Check units and site conditions.

sections.heading: Lifting and concrete
sections.text: Lifting plant includes mobile and tower cranes and hoists. A lifting plan states the load, the safe working load (SWL), the slinging method and the exclusion zone. Never stand under a suspended load. Concrete plant covers batching, mixing, transport, placing and vibrating. A pump speeds placing; a vibrator removes trapped air, but over-vibration causes segregation. Inspect slings and hooks before use.

sections.heading: Temporary works and layout
sections.text: Formwork is the mould holding wet concrete until it can stand; it must be strong, stiff and tight. Striking time (removing the formwork) depends on mix and member. Scaffolding gives a working platform; it needs firm footings, ties, guardrails and toe boards. Excavation support, such as shoring or a trench box, prevents collapse. Site layout places access, storage, plant and welfare safely. Plant regulations and inspection rules differ by country: the UK has LOLER and PUWER, Nigeria has the Factories Act, and COREN registers engineers. Check current local rules.

keyPoints: Plant output = load volume × cycles per hour × efficiency.
Match earthmoving plant to material and haul distance.
Compaction raises density and reduces settlement.
Lifting plans state load, SWL and exclusion zone; never stand under a load.
Formwork and scaffolding must be designed, inspected and maintained.
Plant regulations and inspection intervals differ by country; check local law.

en.title: Measurement and Quantity Taking
en.short: Taking off quantities from drawings, units, descriptions, waste and bill of quantities structure.

sections.heading: Taking off
sections.text: Taking off means measuring quantities from building drawings and specifications. The taker-off reads plans, sections and details, records dimensions in a standard order, and groups work by trade. A dimension paper usually has columns for timesing, dimension, squaring and description. Timesing multiplies repeated items. Squaring calculates the quantity. Accuracy depends on clear drawings and a consistent method.

sections.heading: Units and descriptions
sections.text: Quantities use units that match the work: length in metres (m), area in square metres (m²), volume in cubic metres (m³), countable items in number (nr), and mass in kilograms (kg) or tonnes (t). Some work is measured as an item or sum. A description must identify the material, size, quality and workmanship so the price is unambiguous. For example, concrete of a stated grade in pad foundations is clearer than concrete.

sections.heading: Waste and example
sections.text: Waste is an allowance for cutting, breakage and unavoidable loss. It is not the same as design contingency. Example: a wall 4.0 m long and 2.5 m high has gross area 10.0 m². A door opening 0.9 m × 2.1 m = 1.89 m² is deducted, leaving 8.11 m². With a made-up 5% waste allowance: 8.11 × 1.05 = 8.5155, say 8.52 m². Check: 8.11 + 0.4055 = 8.5155.

sections.heading: Bill structure and standards
sections.text: A bill of quantities (BOQ) lists work with descriptions and quantities so tenderers price the same items. It commonly has preliminaries, measured works grouped by trade, provisional and prime cost sums, and a summary. Standard methods of measurement differ by country and edition. The UK’s RICS publishes measurement rules. In Nigeria, as in other Commonwealth countries, contracts often name a Standard Method of Measurement, but the edition and local amendments vary. Check the current method named in the contract.

keyPoints: Taking off means measuring quantities from drawings and specifications.
Use m, m², m³, nr, kg or t according to the work.
Net quantity = gross quantity − deductions; with waste = net × (1 + waste rate).
Descriptions must state material, size, quality and workmanship.
A BOQ usually has preliminaries, measured works, provisional sums and a summary.
Standard methods of measurement differ by country and edition, so check the current one.

en.title: Estimating and Cost Planning
en.short: Covers design-stage estimates, rates, preliminaries, contingency, cash flow and tender pricing.

sections.heading: Design stages
sections.text:
A cost estimate is a forecast of the likely price of building work. At concept stage an order-of-magnitude estimate uses floor area and a benchmark rate per square metre. As drawings develop, a preliminary estimate prices main elements, then a detailed estimate measures quantities and applies unit rates. A tender price is the contractor’s offer to carry out the work. Accuracy improves with design information, but every estimate remains a forecast.

Rates must match the place and date. Labour, material, plant and subcontract prices change with inflation, exchange rates and taxes. Check current supplier quotations and official tax rules for the country; do not copy old rates.

sections.heading: Rates and allowances
sections.text: A unit rate is the cost of one measured unit, such as per cubic metre of concrete. An all-in labour rate adds wages and statutory employment costs such as pensions and insurance. Material pricing adds delivery and waste. Preliminaries are site-wide costs not measured in the work, such as site office, supervision, insurance and temporary services. Contingency is an allowance for unknown items; it is not a hidden profit margin. Tender pricing also covers overheads and profit.

sections.heading: Worked estimate
sections.text: Example with invented rates: a 50 m² slab, 0.15 m thick, is 50 × 0.15 = 7.5 m³. Concrete at 90,000 per m³ costs 675,000; labour at 25,000 per m³ costs 187,500. Direct cost = 862,500. Add preliminaries at 10% = 86,250 and contingency at 5% = 43,125. Estimate = 862,500 + 86,250 + 43,125 = 991,875 currency units. Real rates and taxes differ by time and place.

sections.heading: Cash flow and tender
sections.text: A cash flow forecast shows money in and out month by month. Contractors often spend before interim payments arrive, so they need working capital. Tender pricing sets the offer: direct costs plus preliminaries, overheads, contingency and profit, adjusted for risk and competition. A low tender may win work but fail if it omits real costs.

keyPoints: Estimates become more accurate as design information increases: order-of-magnitude, preliminary, detailed, then tender.
A unit rate prices one measured unit; an all-in labour rate includes wages and statutory employment costs.
Preliminaries are site-wide costs; contingency is an allowance for unknowns, not profit.
Estimate = direct cost + preliminaries + contingency, with overheads and profit added for a tender price.
Cash flow = money received − money spent in each period; negative months need working capital.
Prices, taxes and regulations change by country and year, so use current quotations and official rules.

en.title: Construction Planning and Scheduling
en.short: Work breakdown, sequencing, bar charts, critical path, resource levelling and progress control.

sections.heading: Work breakdown and sequence
sections.text: Planning starts with a work breakdown structure (WBS), a hierarchy that divides the project into manageable work packages. Each package becomes an activity with a clear output, duration and resource need. Activity sequencing sets the logic: which activities must follow others, which can run in parallel, and which depend on a delivery or inspection. A bar chart, often called a Gantt chart, then places activities against a time axis. It is easy to read on site, but it shows time better than logic.

sections.heading: Critical path method
sections.text:
The critical path method (CPM) builds a network from the same logic. Each activity has a duration. The longest path through the network is the critical path; its length is the shortest possible project duration. Activities on it have zero float. Float is the spare time an activity can use without delaying the project.

Example: A takes 3 days. B takes 4 days after A. C takes 2 days after A. D takes 5 days after B and C. E takes 2 days after D. Path A-B-D-E takes 3 + 4 + 5 + 2 = 14 days. Path A-C-D-E takes 3 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 12 days. The critical path is A-B-D-E at 14 days, and C has 2 days float. Float = latest start − earliest start, or latest finish − earliest finish.

sections.heading: Resource levelling and control
sections.text: Resource levelling adjusts activity timing to reduce peaks in labour, plant or money. It moves non-critical work within its float. If float is too small, levelling can extend the project, so the planner must compare cost and time. Progress monitoring compares planned with actual work using site records, measured quantities, milestones and updated bar charts or networks. Planning supports site control because it sets the sequence, targets and resource calls; monitoring then shows delay, and the programme is revised. Codes, contracts and professional registration differ by country, so check the current local requirements.

keyPoints: A WBS divides the project into work packages that become activities.
Activity sequencing sets dependencies; a bar chart shows timing, while a network shows logic.
The critical path is the longest path through the network and sets the shortest project duration.
Float = latest start − earliest start = latest finish − earliest finish.
Resource levelling moves work within float to reduce peaks and may extend the project if float is insufficient.
Progress monitoring compares actual with planned work and updates the programme to support site control.

en.title: Building Contracts and Procurement
en.short: Procurement routes, tendering, contract types, bills of quantities, variations, payment, claims, delay and disputes.

sections.heading: Procurement routes
sections.text: Procurement is how a client obtains design and construction. In traditional (design-bid-build), the client appoints a designer, then tenders the work to a contractor. In design and build, one firm is responsible for both design and construction. Management contracting and construction management use specialist managers and overlapping packages. Each shifts risk differently: traditional gives the client more design control but can be slower; design and build transfers more risk to the contractor. Names and procedures differ by country.

sections.heading: Tendering and bills
sections.text: Tendering invites offers. Open tendering lets anyone apply; selective tendering shortlists firms; negotiated tendering talks to one or few. A bill of quantities (BOQ) lists measured items with descriptions and quantities. Tenderers price each item, so bids are compared on the same basis. The BOQ also supports interim payments and variation valuation. Errors in quantities are usually corrected under the contract, but rules differ.

sections.heading: Contract types and payment
sections.text: Common contract types are lump sum, re-measurement, cost plus and target cost. A lump sum fixes a price for defined work. Re-measurement pays for actual quantities at tendered rates. Cost plus pays allowable cost plus a fee. Target cost shares savings or overspend against an agreed target. Payment is often monthly by interim certificates after valuation, with retention (a percentage of each payment withheld until the work is complete) held. Example: a BOQ rate is ₦8,500/m²; an instructed extra 15 m² is valued at 15 × 8,500 = ₦127,500, if the rate still applies.

sections.heading: Variations, claims and disputes
sections.text: A variation is a change to the work after contract. It should be instructed and valued by contract rates or agreement. A claim asks for more money or time because of an event, such as late information or abnormal weather. Delays may be excusable (time only) or compensable (time and money); liquidated damages (a pre-agreed sum payable for late completion) may apply to culpable delay, that is delay the contractor caused. Disputes go through negotiation, mediation, adjudication, arbitration or litigation. Construction law and standard forms (for example JCT and NEC in the UK, FIDIC internationally) differ by country, so check the governing law and current edition.

keyPoints: Procurement route allocates design responsibility and risk between client and contractor.
Open, selective and negotiated tendering differ in competition and shortlisting.
A BOQ gives common priced quantities for tendering, payment and variations.
Lump sum, re-measurement, cost plus and target cost contracts allocate price risk differently.
Variations and claims must follow the contract’s notice, valuation and time rules.
Contract law and standard forms differ by country; check the governing law and current edition.

en.title: Building Law and Regulation: Permits, Safety and Compliance
en.short: Covers planning permission, building control, permits, inspections, fire safety, accessibility and environmental rules.

sections.heading: Planning permission
sections.text: Planning permission is approval from the local planning authority to use land or erect or alter a building. It checks zoning, which is the rule for what may be built where, plus density, setbacks, height and access. In Nigeria, planning permission is handled mainly by state or local planning authorities, and the names and forms differ. A developer usually submits site plans, architectural drawings and ownership documents. Approval can carry conditions. Always check the current state planning law and local authority rules.

sections.heading: Building control and permits
sections.text: Building control is the public system that checks construction against safety, health and structural rules. A building permit is the formal permission to start work. Inspections are visits at set stages, such as foundation, slab and completion, to confirm the work matches approved drawings. In Nigeria, the National Building Code is a model code, while enforcement is largely by state and local agencies, so practice varies. Do not assume one state’s permit covers another.

sections.heading: Fire, access and environment
sections.text: Fire safety rules aim to protect life: safe escape routes, fire doors, alarms, extinguishers and access for fire engines. Accessibility rules require usable routes, ramps, toilets and entrances for people with disabilities. Environmental requirements may cover drainage, waste, pollution, energy and an environmental impact assessment (EIA), which predicts likely effects before approval. In Nigeria, the EIA Act and NESREA, the national environmental regulator, are relevant, but thresholds and procedures must be checked.

sections.heading: Case and caution
sections.text: Made-up case: Ngozi plans a two-storey clinic in Enugu, Nigeria. She checks zoning, obtains planning permission, then a building permit with approved drawings. The site is inspected at foundation, slab and completion. She adds a ramp and accessible toilet, fire exits and alarms, and a drainage plan. Final approval may require certificates from the fire and environmental authorities. Requirements change, so confirm with the current national and local authorities.

keyPoints: Planning permission controls land use and building form; building control checks safety and compliance.
A building permit authorises work, and stage inspections verify it against approved drawings.
Fire safety protects escape and firefighting access; accessibility removes barriers for people with disabilities.
Environmental rules may require drainage, waste and pollution controls, and sometimes an EIA.
In Nigeria, the National Building Code is a model and enforcement varies by state and local authority.
Always check the current national and local law, because codes, fees and procedures differ by country and year.

en.title: Professional practice and ethics in building
en.short: Roles, registration, duties, liability, ethics and sustainability in building practice.

sections.heading: Who does what
sections.text: On a building project roles overlap but carry different responsibilities. The builder plans and manages construction: methods, programme, quality, safety and coordination on site. The architect leads the design of form, space and function, and often administers the contract. Engineers design structure and services, such as foundations, frames, drainage and electrical systems. The quantity surveyor measures work and manages cost: cost plans, bills of quantities, valuations and final accounts. Early collaboration matters because design changes affect cost, safety and buildability.

sections.heading: Registration and duties
sections.text: Professional registration is a legal matter and rules differ by country. In Nigeria, for example, CORBON regulates registered builders and NIOB is the professional institute; COREN regulates engineering. In the UK, CIOB is a chartered professional body for construction. Registration may be required before using a protected title or offering certain services. Check current official rules. Registered professionals owe duties to clients, employers, the public and the environment: competence, due care, honesty, confidentiality and disclosure of conflicts of interest. They must not certify work they have not inspected.

sections.heading: Liability and ethics
sections.text: Liability can arise in contract, in tort such as negligence, or under statute. A professional may be sued for loss caused by falling below the standard of a reasonably competent practitioner. Many carry professional indemnity insurance, but it does not replace careful work. Ethical codes require integrity, fair dealing, respect for people and avoidance of bribery or misrepresentation. Reporting unsafe work is a public duty. Ethics also means refusing work beyond your competence and keeping knowledge up to date.

sections.heading: Sustainability case
sections.text: Sustainability is a professional duty, not an optional extra. It covers energy and water use, materials, waste, durability, whole-life carbon and social impact. Example: a made-up school project in Kano. The builder proposes reusing crushed concrete as fill; the engineer checks strength and drainage; the quantity surveyor compares cost and maintenance; the architect checks indoor comfort. The team records this. This shows how roles combine to reduce waste without shifting risk to users.

keyPoints: The builder manages construction; the architect leads design; engineers design structure and services; the quantity surveyor manages measurement and cost.
Professional registration and protected titles differ by country, so check the current official rules; CORBON, NIOB and COREN are Nigerian examples, and CIOB is a UK example.
Registered professionals owe duties of competence, care, honesty, confidentiality and public safety to clients and the public.
Liability may arise in contract, in tort such as negligence, or under statute, and professional indemnity insurance does not replace careful work.
Ethical practice includes disclosing conflicts of interest, refusing work beyond your competence, and reporting unsafe work.
Sustainability is part of professional duty: energy, water, materials, waste, whole-life carbon and social impact should be considered together.

en.title: Research and the Final-Year Project
en.short: Choosing a project, reviewing literature, collecting and analysing data, ethics, referencing and report writing.

sections.heading: Choosing a problem
sections.text: A final-year project starts with a problem, not a title. Choose a building-related issue that is narrow, relevant and feasible: you can reach the site, people or documents, and you have time and tools to collect evidence. Use site observations, records, complaints or local practice. Discuss it with your supervisor and write one clear aim and two or three objectives. 'Housing in Nigeria' is too broad; 'dampness in student hostels at one university' can be studied.

sections.heading: Literature review
sections.text: A literature review is a critical summary of what credible authors know, not a list of quotations. Search textbooks, journals, standards and official reports. Record the author, year, title and source for every item you may cite. Group findings by theme, compare authors, and state the gap your project addresses. Name any standard or law from another country as such.

sections.heading: Data and ethics
sections.text:
Match the method to the question. Questionnaires suit many people, interviews give depth, observation and measurement record site conditions, and secondary data (existing records) saves time. Define your population (whole group), sample (part studied) and instrument (your data collection tool); pilot it (test it on a few people) before full use. Analyse numbers with simple counts, means and percentages, and group interview answers into themes. Do not overclaim from a small sample.

Ethics means respecting people and evidence. Obtain informed consent (free agreement after explanation), keep personal data secure, avoid harm, and do not fabricate or alter results. Rules differ by country and institution, so check your department’s approval procedure. Cite every source in one referencing style; presenting others’ words or ideas as your own is plagiarism.

sections.heading: Writing the report
sections.text: Write the report in this order: title page, abstract, introduction, literature review, method, results, discussion, conclusion, references and appendices. The method should let another student repeat your work. The discussion links results to your objectives and literature, and states limitations honestly. Number tables and figures and refer to them in the text. Leave advanced research design, such as complex sampling or statistical modelling, to master’s study.

keyPoints: Start with a narrow, feasible building-related problem and agree clear aims with your supervisor.
A literature review compares credible sources by theme and identifies the gap you will study.
Choose data methods that fit the question, pilot your instrument and analyse simply and honestly.
Ethics requires informed consent, privacy, safety and no fabrication; approval rules differ by country and institution.
Cite every source in one consistent style and write a report another student could repeat.
Keep the design at undergraduate level; advanced research design belongs to master’s study.

en.title: Advanced Construction Technology and Digital Construction
en.short: Industrialised building, prefabrication, modular construction, automation, BIM, procurement and standards.

sections.heading: Industrialised building
sections.text: Industrialised building means making repeated building parts in a factory and assembling them on site. Prefabrication is off-site manufacture of components such as wall panels or bathroom pods. Modular construction goes further: whole room-sized modules are built and finished in a factory, then lifted into place. Benefits include faster erection, more consistent quality, less weather delay and less site waste. Limits include early design freeze, transport and crane capacity, careful joint and tolerance design, and dependence on a reliable factory supply chain.
