A made-up case: 60 bathroom pods are needed and the crane lifts 6 per day, so installation takes 60 ÷ 6 = 10 days, before connections and services.

sections.heading: Automation and BIM
sections.text: Automation uses machines and software to do repetitive tasks, such as computer-controlled cutting, robotic welding or automated layout. Building information modelling (BIM) is a digital model of a building plus structured information about its parts, costs and maintenance. It supports coordination: designers and contractors combine models, detect clashes and share quantities. The ISO 19650 series gives an international approach to managing information through a project and asset life. Benefits are fewer clashes, better decisions and a record for operation. Limits are poor model discipline, training cost, software interoperability and unclear legal reliance on the model.

sections.heading: Procurement and standards
sections.text: Off-site work changes procurement. Early contractor and manufacturer involvement helps, because factory design must be fixed before production. Contracts should state who designs the modules, how approvals and factory inspections happen, how risk and payment are allocated, and what information is exchanged. A BIM protocol or information requirement may be added. Rules differ by country: in Nigeria, COREN registers engineers, and building codes, public procurement rules and contract forms are national or project-specific. Do not assume a foreign standard or clause applies. Check the current official standard, the contract and local registration requirements before relying on a model or a prefabricated system.

keyPoints: Industrialised building moves repeated work from site into a factory.
Prefabrication makes components off site; modular construction makes whole room-sized units.
BIM is a digital model with structured information for coordination and information management.
ISO 19650 is an international information management series, but national guidance and contracts vary.
Off-site manufacture needs early design freeze and clear allocation of design, inspection and payment risk.
Check current national standards, registration rules and contract terms; do not assume foreign clauses apply.

en.title: Sustainable Building Design
en.short: Life-cycle carbon, energy and water efficiency, materials, waste and green rating schemes.

sections.heading: Life-cycle and carbon
sections.text:
Life-cycle thinking judges a building from material extraction through construction, use, maintenance and end of life. Life-cycle assessment (LCA) adds up impacts, often as carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e). Operational carbon comes from energy used in the building; embodied carbon comes from materials, transport, construction and replacement. A low-operational design can raise embodied carbon, so compare whole-life totals.

Example: a made-up office has 120 kWh/m²/yr electricity, a grid factor of 0.4 kg CO2e/kWh and 50 years of use. Operational carbon is 120 × 0.4 × 50 = 2,400 kg CO2e/m². If embodied carbon is 300 kg CO2e/m², operational dominates here. Change the grid factor or lifespan and the balance changes.

sections.heading: Efficiency and materials
sections.text:
Energy efficiency reduces demand first: orientation, shading, insulation, daylight and natural ventilation, then efficient equipment. Water efficiency uses low-flow fittings, leak control, rainwater harvesting and greywater reuse, with treatment and health safeguards. Material selection considers durability, maintenance, recycled content, local availability and toxicity.

No material is best in every case: timber may store carbon but needs responsible sourcing; cement has high embodied carbon but is often structurally necessary. Compare options on function and whole-life impact, not a single label.

sections.heading: Waste and ratings
sections.text:
Waste follows the hierarchy: prevent, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose. Design for disassembly and standard sizes reduces offcuts. Green rating schemes score or certify performance. Examples include BREEAM (United Kingdom), LEED (United States, used internationally), Green Star (Australia and other countries) and EDGE (International Finance Corporation).

They differ in scope, weightings and verification, and local adaptations exist. Regulations also differ by country; check the current official version. A rating is a guide, not a substitute for LCA or local code compliance.

keyPoints: Life-cycle thinking compares impacts from material extraction to end of life, not only use.
Operational carbon = annual energy use × emission factor × years; embodied carbon comes from materials and construction.
A low-operational design can increase embodied carbon, so compare whole-life totals.
Energy efficiency starts with passive design and demand reduction before efficient equipment; water efficiency uses low-flow fittings, leak control and reuse with health safeguards.
Material choice depends on function, durability, maintenance, sourcing and whole-life impact; no material is best in every case.
Use the waste hierarchy and check local regulations and rating schemes, which differ by country and version.

en.title: Building Performance Simulation: Models, Inputs and Critical Use
en.short: Thermal, energy, daylight, ventilation and acoustic modelling: inputs, assumptions, validation and critical reading.

sections.heading: What the models do
sections.text: Building performance simulation (BPS) uses computer models to predict how a building will behave before or after construction. Thermal and energy models divide the building into zones and solve heat balances hour by hour. Daylight models trace sky and sun light; ventilation models range from simple airflow networks to computational fluid dynamics (CFD); acoustic models predict sound paths and reverberation. The output is an estimate, not a measurement. They are used for design, retrofit and compliance studies.

sections.heading: Inputs and assumptions
sections.text: Inputs include geometry, constructions, glazing, weather data (often a typical meteorological year file), occupancy and equipment schedules, internal gains, and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) settings. Each is an assumption. A schedule that says a room is full from 08:00 to 17:00 may be wrong. Weather files describe a typical year, not a forecast. Check units, orientation and zone boundaries. Document every source. Record the software version.

sections.heading: Validation and uncertainty
sections.text: Validation checks whether the model represents reality. Internal checks compare against analytical solutions or test cases. External checks compare predictions with measured energy, temperatures, daylight or sound. Calibration adjusts inputs within measured uncertainty, not to force a match. Sensitivity analysis varies inputs, often one at a time, to see which assumptions matter. Report uncertainty.

sections.heading: Reading results critically
sections.text: Read results critically. A single annual energy figure hides timing and peaks. Look at hourly profiles, comfort hours and unmet loads. Example: a model predicts 12,000 kWh/year for a building; metered use is 15,000 kWh/year. The difference is (15,000 − 12,000) ÷ 15,000 = 20% of measured use. Before tuning, check weather year, occupancy, equipment gains and meter boundaries. Codes and compliance rules differ by country, so check the current local code.

keyPoints: Building performance simulation predicts thermal, energy, daylight, ventilation and acoustic behaviour from a computer model, not from measurement.
Inputs such as weather, schedules, gains and HVAC settings are assumptions; document sources and units.
Validation compares the model with analytical cases, test data or measurements; calibration should stay within uncertainty.
Sensitivity analysis shows which inputs change the result most, so effort goes to the inputs that are both influential and uncertain.
Percentage difference = (measured − predicted) ÷ measured × 100.
Codes and compliance limits differ by country; check the current local code.

en.title: Research Methods for Building
en.short: Designing, sampling, analysing, writing and defending a master’s building research dissertation.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text: A research design connects a question to evidence. Start with a focused question, a literature review and a conceptual framework. Quantitative design measures variables and tests hypotheses with numbers, such as a survey of classroom temperatures. Qualitative design explores meanings and processes, such as interviews with site supervisors about safety. Mixed methods combine both, often using interviews to explain survey results. Building research may use experiment, survey, case study, interview or document analysis. State the unit of analysis, such as a building, firm or worker, and define variables before collecting data.

sections.heading: Sampling and measurement
sections.text:
Sampling selects part of a population to represent the whole. A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn. Probability methods, such as random, stratified and cluster sampling, allow estimates of error. Non-probability methods, such as convenience and purposive sampling, are common in qualitative work but limit generalisation. Measurement needs operational definitions, validity (does it measure the concept?) and reliability (is it consistent?). Variables may be nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio.

For a proportion, n = z²p(1 − p) ÷ e². With 95% confidence, z = 1.96, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05:
n = 1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so collect about 385 responses. For small populations, apply a finite population correction.

sections.heading: Analysis, ethics and writing
sections.text: Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics and inferential tests chosen for the data type and design. Qualitative analysis often uses coding and thematic analysis. Mixed methods need integration, not two separate studies. Ethics approval is required before collecting data from people. Obtain informed consent, protect anonymity and confidentiality, avoid harm, store data securely and follow the data protection law of the country concerned. In building research, site safety and commercial confidentiality need care. Write clearly, justify method choices, report limitations honestly and use a consistent referencing style. In the defence, explain how design, sampling, measurement, analysis and ethics answer the question.

keyPoints: A research design must match the question, the evidence and the time available.
Quantitative methods test hypotheses with numbers; qualitative methods explore meanings and processes; mixed methods integrate both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling limits it.
Measurement needs operational definitions, validity and reliability.
For a proportion, n = z²p(1 − p) ÷ e²; with 95% confidence, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05, n is about 385.
Ethics approval, informed consent, confidentiality and data protection are required before collecting data from people.
